chunks: Timer applications in embedded systems. The question: What are some applications?
Nearly every embedded product, meaning a device with a small built-in computer, uses timers.
The most common use is a steady tick, once per millisecond, that slower jobs hang off: blinking an LED, debouncing a button, timing out a reply.
Timers also make PWM, which is rapid on-off switching used for dimming lights and controlling motors. They also measure pulses and reset a frozen chip.
Picture an orchestra with a conductor who gives one steady beat.
Each section keeps its own count of beats, and plays when its turn comes: strings every two beats, brass every eight.
The conductor is the one hardware timer, and each section is a software timer that is just a number compared against the beat count.
But a section cannot play between beats, so the beat limits how fine the timing can be.
One hardware timer fans out into many software timers.
Each software timer is just a variable and a comparison, so you can have dozens at almost no cost; the only limit is the tick resolution.
System tick: a regular timer interrupt, a signal that briefly pauses the main program (see "What interrupts are"), often every 1 milliseconds, used as the software's time base.
Software timer: a stored deadline compared with the tick count. Debounce: ignoring a switch's rapid flicker by requiring a steady state for a set time.
PWM (pulse-width modulation): switching a pin on and off fast, so the average power follows the fraction of time it is on.
Watchdog: a timer that resets the chip if software forgets to restart it, which catches a hang.
Set a hardware timer to a 1 kilohertz tick. Its interrupt routine only adds 1 to a millisecond counter. If it takes 5 microseconds, it uses 5 micro s times 1000 equals 0.
5 % of the processor. For a button: sample it every millisecond, and accept a change only after 20 samples in a row agree, so 20 milliseconds of stable signal.
The rule of thumb is to use hardware timers for tight timing and software timers for slow jobs. That is the whole idea.

"The big ones are the system tick, which drives scheduling, debounce and timeouts; PWM for LEDs, motors, servos and converters; and input capture for measuring things like an ultrasonic echo or a tachometer to a microsecond.
Timers can also trigger the ADC at an exact rate so sampling has no software jitter. And the special timers, the watchdog for fault recovery and the RTC for low-power wake-ups.
In every case I choose a hardware timer when timing is tight and a software timer on the tick when it's slow."
